title: One Poisoned Bottle
problem: Exactly one of 1,000 bottles is poisoned. You have 10 test strips and may place drops from any bottles on each strip. After one simultaneous round, each strip reports only positive or negative. How can you identify the poisoned bottle?

hints.text: Ten binary outcomes can encode more than 1,000 distinct identities.
Number the bottles and associate each test strip with one bit of the bottle number.

solution.setup: Number bottles 0 through 999 and write each number as a 10-bit binary string.
solution.reasoning: For each bottle, place a drop on exactly those strips corresponding to 1-bits in its binary label. After testing, interpret positive strips as 1 and negative strips as 0. The resulting 10-bit pattern is precisely the poisoned bottle's label. Ten strips distinguish 2^10=1024 patterns, enough for 1,000 bottles.
solution.finalAnswer: Use the strips as the ten bits of a binary code; the positive/negative pattern identifies the bottle in one round.
solution.sanityCheck: Because 2^9=512<1000, nine binary strips could not guarantee identification, while ten can.

keyInsight: Parallel yes/no tests can encode candidate identities rather than testing candidates individually.
recognitionCues: A one-round identification problem with binary outcomes suggests binary encoding.
commonMistakes: Dividing bottles into only ten disjoint groups, which identifies a group but not a bottle.
followUps: How many bottles can 12 strips distinguish?
How would a delayed or unreliable positive result change the design?

source.notes: Original formulation of a standard binary-testing puzzle family.

verification.notes: Every bottle receives a unique 10-bit code.
